A pine is a type of tree — specifically, an evergreen tree that belongs to a large family of trees called Pinus. "Evergreen" means it stays green all year long, even through winter, because it never completely sheds its leaves the way most trees do in autumn.

The word "pine" can refer to the tree itself, or to the wood that comes from it. Both uses are common and equally standard.
What a pine tree looks like

Pine trees are among the most recognizable trees in the world. Here are their defining characteristics:

Needle-shaped leaves. Instead of the broad, flat leaves that most trees have, pines have long, thin, sharp leaves called pine needles. These needles are green, slender, and pointy. They grow in small bundles or clusters attached to the branches — usually 2, 3, or 5 needles per bundle, depending on the species. This bundled arrangement is one of the surest ways to identify a pine tree.

Pine cones. Pines produce hard, woody, scaly structures called pine cones (or cones). These are the tree's seed-bearing organs — the equivalent of fruit in other trees, but much harder and drier. A pine cone starts out small, green, and soft, but as it matures, it becomes brown, dry, and stiff. Hidden between its overlapping scales are the seeds. When the cone dries out and opens up, the seeds fall or are released. Pine cones are so strongly associated with pine trees that people use the two words almost interchangeably in everyday life ("I found a pine cone in the garden").

Shape and height. Most pine trees are tall and have a roughly conical or pointed shape — think of a Christmas tree silhouette. However, older pines and some species can become more irregular or umbrella-shaped. Many pines grow anywhere from 10 to 70 metres (about 30 to 230 feet) tall, though dwarf varieties exist too.

Bark. The bark of a pine tree is usually rough and scaly, often grayish-brown or reddish-brown. If you scratch or cut through the bark, a sticky, syrupy liquid called resin (or sap) oozes out. This resin has a strong, distinctive, sharp, woody smell — the classic "pine smell" that you might recognise from forests, pine-scented cleaning products, or certain air fresheners.

Pine trees are native to the Northern Hemisphere — meaning they naturally grow across North America, Europe, Asia, and parts of North Africa. They are remarkably adaptable: some species thrive in cold mountain regions and subarctic climates, while others grow in warm, dry, sandy coastal areas. Pine forests cover enormous stretches of land in countries like Russia, Canada, the United States, Scandinavia, China, and India (the Himalayas, for instance, have dense pine forests).

Because of their hardiness and usefulness, pine trees have also been planted by humans in the Southern Hemisphere — in countries like South Africa, Australia, Brazil, and New Zealand — where they are not naturally found but are cultivated for their timber.

When people talk about "pine" in the context of building, furniture, or carpentry, they are talking about the wood of the pine tree.

Pine wood is one of the most widely used types of wood in the world. Here is why:

  • It is softwood, which means it is easier to cut, shape, and work with than hardwoods like oak or teak. (The term "softwood" does not mean the wood is weak — it simply refers to the type of tree it comes from.)
  • It is relatively affordable, because pine trees grow quickly and are widely available.
  • It is lightweight yet sturdy enough for most everyday purposes.
  • It has a straight grain and a clean, pale, yellowish-cream colour, often with visible reddish-brown knots (the circular patterns where branches once grew). This appearance is considered attractive and rustic by many people.

Pine is used to make furniture (tables, chairs, wardrobes), flooring, doors, window frames, house frames, fences, and paper pulp.
Products that come from pine trees

Beyond the wood, pine trees give us several other useful things:

Resin and turpentine. The sticky resin that flows from a pine tree has been harvested for centuries. When distilled (processed through heat), it produces turpentine, a liquid used as a solvent for paints and varnishes.

Pine oil. Extracted from pine needles and wood, pine oil is used in disinfectants, cleaning sprays, and aromatherapy. That sharp, clean smell in many floor cleaners and bathroom sprays is pine oil.

Pine nuts. Certain species of pine, especially the stone pine (Pinus pinea) found in Mediterranean regions and the pinyon pine in North America, produce large, edible seeds inside their cones. These seeds are what we call pine nuts — the small, creamy, tear-drop-shaped nuts you find in pesto sauce and various cuisines.

Pine tar. A thick, dark substance produced by heating pine wood without oxygen, pine tar has been used historically for waterproofing ships, ropes, and roofs, and it still appears in some soaps and treatments for skin conditions.
How many kinds of pine are there?

There are roughly 120 species of pine trees, all belonging to the genus Pinus. You do not need to know all of them, but some of the most well-known include:

  • Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) — the only pine native to the British Isles, with distinctive orange-red bark on the upper trunk.
  • Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus) — a tall, graceful pine native to eastern North America, known for its long, soft needles and slender cones.
  • Stone pine (Pinus pinea) — the classic umbrella-shaped pine of Mediterranean landscapes, famous for producing pine nuts.
  • Lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta) — common in western North America, often densely packed in mountain forests.
  • Himalayan blue pine (Pinus wallichiana) — found in the Himalayas, with very long, drooping, bluish-green needles.

Each species has slightly different needles, cones, bark, and growing preferences, but they all share the essential characteristics described above.
Pine in compound words and phrases

The word "pine" appears inside several common words and phrases, which is worth knowing to avoid confusion:

Pineapple — This fruit is called a "pineapple" because when European explorers first saw it in the Americas in the 15th century, they thought it looked like a large pine cone (pine + apple, the old English word for any fruit). The two plants are entirely unrelated, but the name stuck.

Pine forest / pine grove — A stretch of land covered with pine trees.

Pine cone — As explained above, the seed-bearing structure of the pine tree.

Pine needle — A single leaf of a pine tree.

Pine resin / pine sap — The sticky liquid produced by the tree.
A quick note on the "pine scent"

The distinctive smell of pine — sharp, fresh, green, slightly medicinal — comes from natural chemical compounds in the tree's resin and needles called terpenes (specifically alpha-pinene and beta-pinene, named after the tree itself). This smell has become so culturally embedded with ideas of cleanliness, freshness, and nature that it is deliberately added to hundreds of products, from cleaning sprays to candles to car air fresheners.

As a noun, pine means:

  1. A type of evergreen, cone-bearing tree with needle-shaped leaves, found mainly in the Northern Hemisphere, with about 120 species worldwide.
  2. The wood that comes from that tree, widely used in construction, furniture, and papermaking.

Everything that flows from the word — pine cones, pine needles, pine resin, pine oil, pine nuts, pine forests — traces back to this one tree. It is one of the most economically important and visually iconic trees on Earth, and its scent and image are instantly recognizable across most of the world.
